title: Migration Quality Assurance
learning_outcomes: Explain migration quality assurance and connect it to at least two of its syllabus subtopics.
Apply migration quality assurance in a small SCSS example and predict the resulting CSS or compiler behavior.
Inspect the output, diagnose one plausible mistake, and state a relevant limitation or best practice.

content.intro: This lesson turns **Migration Quality Assurance** into a practical, inspectable step. You will connect comparing pre-migration and post-migration css with detecting changed selector output, then check what Dart Sass emits instead of relying on the SCSS source alone.
content.why_it_matters: The Sass module system separates member definitions from their use: `@use` provides namespaced access and loads a module once, while `@forward` exposes selected members through a library entrypoint. This makes dependency direction and public APIs easier to review.

content_blocks.title: The mental model
content_blocks.text: For new work, prefer Dart Sass and the module system. Keep legacy patterns only when maintaining an older codebase, migrate in small batches, and compare compiled CSS because a successful compile does not alone guarantee equivalent output.

items.title: Comparing pre-migration and post-migration CSS
items.text: Migrate incrementally, prefer current Dart Sass modules, inspect warnings, and compare before/after CSS. Automated migration still requires code review and tests.

items.title: Detecting changed selector output
items.text: Predict the expanded selector before compiling. Keep nesting shallow and verify that the emitted selector does not match more elements than intended.

items.title: Resolving namespace collisions
items.text: Show where the member is defined and how consumers reach it. Namespaced `@use` is the modern default; `@forward` exposes a curated API, and legacy `@import` is deprecated.

items.title: Managing third-party package compatibility
items.text: For managing third-party package compatibility, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation.

items.title: Verifying warnings and errors
items.text: Reproduce the issue with the smallest entrypoint, read the first relevant diagnostic, fix the source rather than the generated file, and recompile to verify the correction.

items.title: Documenting completed migrations
items.text: Migrate incrementally, prefer current Dart Sass modules, inspect warnings, and compare before/after CSS. Automated migration still requires code review and tests.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with the smallest source file that demonstrates migration quality assurance. 2. State what should change and what should stay the same. 3. Compile the entrypoint with Dart Sass, or use the stated command if this lesson is about the toolchain. 4. Compare the resulting CSS or diagnostic with the expected result, then change one input and repeat.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Migration Quality Assurance
content_blocks.code:
npx sass src/scss/main.scss /tmp/after.css
# Compare /tmp/after.css with a saved pre-migration CSS baseline.
content_blocks.expected_output: A CSS diff highlights output changes; review meaningful differences instead of assuming every whitespace change is a behavior change.
content_blocks.execution_note: This course example is a Sass/SCSS or tooling example. CodeLeaf’s current in-browser playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; compile Sass locally with Dart Sass. Do not treat the browser preview as a Sass compiler.

content_blocks.title: Modern Sass note
content_blocks.text: Use Dart Sass for new work. Prefer @use / @forward and namespaced sass: built-in modules. Sass compiles to CSS; browser-native CSS features still run in the browser.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Audit a small stylesheet for migration quality assurance. Save the original source and compiled CSS, make one deliberate change, recompile, and write down the evidence that the change is correct and safe.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Do not edit generated CSS when you intend to change source behavior. Edit the SCSS entrypoint or its module, compile again, and compare the generated output.

task_acceptance_criteria: The example includes the intended Sass construct and a clear input.
The expected output or tool result is documented and consistent with the source.
The work is reproducible and includes one limitation, test, or troubleshooting note.
hints: Reduce the example to one source file and one entrypoint before adding more abstractions.
Read the first compiler diagnostic and confirm you are editing the Sass source, not only generated CSS.
Compile and inspect the emitted CSS; compare exact selectors, values, and at-rules with your expectation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming SCSS runs directly in the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Browsers consume CSS, not Sass syntax.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with Dart Sass and load the resulting .css file in the HTML page.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting source readability without inspecting generated output.
common_mistakes.why: Nesting, mixins, loops, and extension can emit unexpected selectors or more CSS than intended.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile a small example and inspect the CSS output or browser computed styles.

summary: Migration Quality Assurance is useful when it solves the specific organization or reuse problem described in this lesson.
Keep compile-time Sass behavior distinct from browser-time CSS behavior.
Validate both source intent and generated CSS before relying on the pattern in a larger project.
